-scale anisotropies of cosmic rays
with energies above 4 EeV measured using the Pierre Auger Observatory. For the
energy bins [4,8] EeV and $E\geq 8$ EeV, the most significant signal is a
dipolar modulation in right ascension at energies above 8 EeV, as previously
reported. In this paper we further scrutinize the highest-energy bin by
splitting it into three energy ranges. We find that the amplitude of the dipole
increases with energy above 4 EeV. The growth can be fitted with a power law
with index $\beta=0.79\pm 0.19$. The directions of the dipoles are consistent
with an extragalactic origin of these anisotropies at all the energies
considered. Additionally we have estimated the quadrupolar components of the
anisotropy: they are not statistically significant. We discuss the results in
the context of the predictions from different models for the distribution of
ultrahigh-energy sources and cosmic magnetic fields.
  Finally, we update the limits on the density of cosmic magnetic fields in the
local universe, starting from the exclusion of magnetic deflections inducing
more than 30$^{\circ}$ difference between arrival directions of two particles
separated by less than $2^{\circ}$ in the sky, to $\rho_B \lesssim 2.8 \times
10^{-16}$ G ${\rm cm^{-3}}$ for a magnetized source distribution, and to
$\rho_B \lesssim 1.6 \times 10^{-16}$ G ${\rm cm^{-3}}$ assuming that sources
are uniformly distributed across the sky.

problem can be reformulated as an ordinary quantum problem in a commuting
momentum space. The coordinates are then represented as linear differential
operators $\hat x_a = -i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab} (p)\, \partial /\partial p_b $.

(so(1,1)) yields interesting generalizations of the Lorentz transformation.

semiclassical approach when $\theta$ is small, for quantum systems where the
parameter is the only small scale (e.g. a particle on a sphere).

cable causes four spectral nulls on the 36GHz bandwidth of 72Gbit/s OOK signal,
which is the main obstacle for achieving an acceptable bit-error-rate (BER)
performance. Decision feedback equalizer (DFE) is effective to compensate for
the spectral nulls. However, DFE has a serious defect of burst-error
propagation when the burst errors emerge due to the unstable submarine
environment. Weighted DFE (WDFE) can be used to mitigate the burst-error
propagation, but it cannot fully compensate for the spectral nulls because only
a part of feedback symbols is directly decided. Fortunately, maximum likelihood
sequence estimation (MLSE) can be added after the WDFE to simultaneously
eliminate the resisting spectral distortions and implement optimal detection.
Compared to the joint DFE and MLSE algorithm, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm
can effectively suppress the burst-error propagation to obtain a maximum 2.9dB
improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ factor and eliminate the phenomenon of BER
floor. In conclusion, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm can be effectively
adopted to compensate for the spectral nulls of 72Gbit/s OOK signal transmitted
over 18.8km submarine optical cable. Besides, the joint WDFE and MLSE
algorithm can be extended to the 100Gbit/s OOK system to obtain similar
improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ factor.

the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional
dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories
about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing
values, we make no assumptions on their existence: a missing value exists only
if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table.

with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown;
and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as
consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to
mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query
answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last
decades.

approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional
dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and
false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and
Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel
solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.

  Object manipulation tasks can be demonstrated to a robot by providing direct
control of the end-effector. An alternative and more interesting supervision
strategy is to provide suboptimal feedback, mimicking human performance that
inherently contains noise and bias. For example, a user may need to retry
multiple times to complete a task, or may themselves make errors while
demonstrating it. The question then arises of how much such supervision
degrades the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms. We study this
issue on a set of manipulation tasks that require precise geometric contact,
and find that multiple iterations as well as human error significantly
degrade performance. A small modification, namely prioritized rewriting of
transition samples, makes the learning of such tasks more robust to
suboptimal feedback. Our method achieves this by reducing the sample complexity
of the transition function of the subtask of grasp pose estimation, which is a
critical component of the object manipulation task. In addition, our method
makes better use of near-successes, which are particularly common when
manipulating real objects. We also study our method on a set of simulated
scenarios that ask repeated use of multiple objects, and show that our method
makes fewer samples than baseline methods while achieving high performance.

Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2) using high-resolution near-infrared spectra collected
with the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II survey
(APOGEE-2), obtained as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. We investigate
chemical abundances for a variety of species including the light-, odd-Z,
$\alpha$-, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements from high S/N spectra of seven
giant members. The derived mean cluster metallicity is [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$,
with no evidence for an intrinsic metallicity spread. Ton~2 exhibits a typical
$\alpha$-enrichment that follows the trend for high-metallicity Galactic GCs,
similar to that seen in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. We find a significant nitrogen
spread ($>0.87$ dex), and a large fraction of nitrogen-enriched stars that
populate the cluster. Given the relatively high-metallicity of Ton~2, these
nitrogen-enriched stars are well above the typical Galactic levels, indicating
the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon in this cluster which also
contains several stars with typical low, first-generation N abundances. We also
identify the presence of [Ce/Fe] $>$ 0 and [Eu/Fe] $>$ 0 in several N-enriched
stars, suggesting that the neutron-capture process in the bulge/GC population is
not purely driven by the r-process. Furthermore, the relationship between [N/C]
and [O/N] indicates that the nitrogen and oxygen production mechanisms are not
independent. Lastly, we find that the CNO enrichment in Ton~2 follows a path
consistent with the increasing contribution of the triple-$\alpha$ reaction as
the cluster metallicity increases.

and its relation to the accreted satellite populations of the Milky Way galaxy.
We propose that the N-enriched stars in Ton~2 likely result from the stellar
generations born from primordial or early-generation CNO-enriched, extreme
horizontal branch (EHB) stars, which in turn formed through the merger of

has grown to a significant size in the
past years. It makes up for an impressive body of research, which enables a
number of statistical approaches to various aspects in theorem proving, and has
not yet been utilized exhaustively. However, the growing size also poses some
challenges to address: Material becomes increasingly harder to find,
reusability and ease of understanding become more important. This thesis
abstract summarizes my research plans on those topics and briefly touches on
preliminary results, which indicate that the node in-degree of the dependency
graph of the archive follows a scale-free distribution.
  My plans are divided into three main parts: (1) I want to address the problem
of archive navigation with a number of techniques from information retrieval
and graph theory. My goal is to provide a search engine for the archive,
together with a search interface, which uses natural language processing to
enable easy-to-understand search queries. (2) Based on the statistics obtained
from the in-degree distribution, I want to analyze the structure of the archive
and provide recommendations on how to improve it. My main tool for this will be
a parametric model of the in-degree distribution from graph theory, which I
will estimate from the data. (3) Finally, I want to provide a collection of
tools around a core proof graph query language, which enables users to
conveniently answer common questions like "Which theorems prove exactly those
and those lemmas?" or "Which theorems rely on exactly three lemmas?" Based on
this query language, I will provide a number of utilities to make handling the
output of the queries even easier.
  In summary, my plans for the next months are filled to the brim with
opportunities for interesting statistical investigations and useful
applications for the archive. I am looking forward to working on them and am
open for any suggestions and ideas from fellow researchers.
  As final note, I want to invite everyone to a workshop on "Statistical
Analysis of Formal Proofs" at the CADE conference in Lake Como next year. The
workshop aims at bringing together researchers from the fields of theorem
proving, artificial intelligence, computer science, mathematics and statistics
to discuss the methods and applications of statistical techniques in
theorem proving and vice versa. I am planning on reporting my results from the
next months in a paper and I am happy to discuss ideas and feedback on the
topic.

experiments in high-energy astrophysics is seemingly straightforward, but
reaching high precision of the order of 0.01 in the determination of the
vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) has proven difficult. Wide-field
photometry over a large span of altitudes allows a fast determination of VAOD
independently of the absolute calibration of the system, while providing this
calibration as a useful by-product. Using several years of data taken by the
FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre
Auger Observatory in Argentina and about a year of data taken by a similar
instrument deployed at the planned future Southern site of the Cherenkov
Telescope Array in Chile, we have developed methods to improve the precision of
this measurement technique towards and possibly beyond the 0.01 mark. Detailed
laboratory measurements of the response of the whole system to both the
spectrum and intensity of incoming light have proven indispensable in this
analysis as the usual assumption of linearity of the CCD detectors is not valid
anymore for the conditions of the observations.
  We present the design and test of a new, higher-sensitivity head of the
system, based on a new, cooler CCD and improvements in optics and calibrators.
We also present a new method to quickly determine the pointing direction of
the telescope to high accuracy from the data themselves, greatly simplifying
the necessary corrections. Finally, we report on the implementation of a number
of operational changes and analysis techniques that all contribute to small
errors in the determined VAOD and show how they all add up towards the
final energy estimate in the context of optical/orical air showers.
  Future tests with different optical systems and possibly better calibrators
will continue to yield new results. In particular, the implementation of a
direct solar calibrator will be critical in this direction.

modeling limitations, is widely employed in numerical simulations, due to its
easy implementation combined with physical intuitiveness and stability. In the

reviewed and investigated. A detailed description of peridynamics theory,
applications and numerical models has been presented. Employed BB-PD integral
kernels have been displayed, together with their differences and commonalities;
then, some consequences of their mathematical structure have been discussed.
The kinematic role of nonlocality, the relation between kernel structure and
material impenetrability, and the role of PD kernel nonlinearity in cracks
formation prediction have been critically analyzed and commented. Finally the
idea of extending BB-PD to fluids is proposed and presented in the framework of
fading memory material, drawing some perspectives for a deeper and more
comprehensive understanding of the peridynamics in fluids.
  The paper is organized as follows: in Section 1 a detailed description of
peridynamics theory, applications and numerical models is presented. In Section
2 the role of kinematic nonlocality in PD models is analyzed and discussed.
Section 3 is devoted to the analysis of the relation between material
impenetrability and PD kernel nonlinearity. In Section 4 cracks formation
prediction and mechanism is analyzed and discussed. Finally in Section 5 some
ideas about PD application to fluids are proposed and presented.

package for solving General Graphical Lasso
problems. The Graphical Lasso scheme, introduced by (Friedman 2007) (see also
(Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008)), estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix
$\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,
\Sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^p$. Originally proposed by (Dempster 1972) under the
name Covariance Selection, this estimation framework has been extended to
include latent variables in (Chandrasekaran 2012). Recent extensions also
include the joint estimation of multiple inverse covariance matrices, see,
e.g., in (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package contains methods for
solving a general problem formulation, including important special cases, such
as, the single (latent variable) Graphical Lasso, the Group, and the Fused
Graphical Lasso.
  GGLasso provides two main algorithms for solving the general Graphical Lasso
problem: a) an algorithm based on, in principle, exact covariance matrix
solutions using Schur complements and b) an algorithm based on iterative
proximal gradient descent steps. Both algorithms can be run in parallel to
explore the entire factorization of the objective function and thus return
multiple sparse estimation candidates. The user may then select the sparsest
solution that best fits the underlying sparsity pattern of interest.

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer of the network and no inter-layer edges. As
in the standard eigenvector centrality construction, the importance of each
node in a given layer is based on the weighted sum of the importance of
adjacent nodes in that same layer. Unlike standard eigenvector centrality, we
assume that the adjacency relationship and the importance of adjacent nodes may
be based on distinct layers. Importantly, this type of centrality constraint is
only partially supported by existing frameworks for multilayer eigenvector
centrality that use edges between nodes in different layers to capture
inter-layer dependencies. For our model, constrained, layer-specific
eigenvector centrality values are defined by a system of independent eigenvalue
problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, whose solution can be
efficiently realized using an interleaved power iteration algorithm.
Moreover, our approach is broad enough to capture both tight and relaxed
constraints on the eigenvector centrality vector, with the latter reflecting
situations in which the importance of adjacent nodes has an independent
impact on the importance of a node. Our approach is also extendable to
incorporate weights on the constrained centrality relationships between nodes as
needed. We demonstrate the usefulness of our method by analyzing the
structural importance of nodes in eight different networks in a variety of
applications, including the presence of communities, the existence of
triangles, and the value of degree variance.

Constraints.

from observational data and domain background knowledge, aimed at causal graph
and causal mechanism modeling. The 'cdt' package implements the end-to-end
approach, recovering the direct dependencies (the skeleton of the causal graph)
and the causal relationships between variables. It includes algorithms from the

discovery such as ANM. 'cdt' is available under the MIT License at

which variables cause which others and how to analyze this graph to answer
users' queries. We show how to learn the underlying causal mechanisms by
specifying interactions in the causal graph and a methodology for encoding
domain knowledge into the graph.
  We compare 'cdt' to other causal discovery frameworks and evaluate the
predictive power of causal models induced by 'cdt' in comparison to other
approaches. The results show that 'cdt' can learn accurate causal graphs and
models, leading to improvements in prediction accuracy.

CausalDiscoveryToolboxEvaluation.

developers of causal discovery algorithms and practitioners who need these
tools to analyze their data. We welcome pull requests from anyone who wishes

largely driven by the collaboration and openness of the community. We share

and algorithms acting on such representations can lead to significant
advances in automation, allowing our 'qd' toolbox to answer users' queries
more generally. We hope that the community will adopt our proposals for
standardizing causal graph representations and the algorithms acting on such
representations.

facilitate specifying a causal graph and analyzing it.

global symmetries that could be present and explore how they are avoided.
Crucial ingredients that arise in such effective field theories are generalized
$\theta$-terms. These introduce non-linear couplings between axion fields and
topological terms quadratic in the gauge field strengths which break a large
subset of the global symmetries. Additional residual global symmetries may
further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we
illustrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms leads to a
generalized Witten effect, which implies that the spectrum of charged states is
constituted by an infinitely populated lattice. We further show that such a
lattice is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that
characterizes the moduli space boundary near which the effective theory is
defined.

conjecture of the absence of global symmetries to effective theories with
non-geometric backgrounds.

for which torsion elements are required to vanish in effective field theories
based on $\mathcal{N} \geq 2$ supersymmetry algebras follow from the absence of
global symmetries plus the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms.

with non-geometric backgrounds can be applied to other theories, such as those
obtained by compactifying Type IIB superstring theory on Calabi-Yau manifolds of
real dimension $d<3$.

show that, depending on how they are realized, some of them may actually
correspond to geometric backgrounds in higher dimensions.

global symmetries can be generalized to other contexts.

\textit{adaptive} adversary who can arbitrarily corrupt the reward and
transition at every step within an episode, for at most $\epsilon$-fraction of
the learning episodes. Our attack model is strictly stronger than those
considered in prior works. Our first result shows that no algorithm can find a
better than $O(\epsilon)$-optimal policy under our attack model. Next, we show
that surprisingly the natural policy gradient (NPG) method retains a natural
robustness property if the reward corruption is bounded, and can find an
$O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. Consequently, we develop a Filtered Policy
Gradient (FPG) algorithm that can tolerate even unbounded reward corruption and
can find an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. We emphasize that FPG is the
first that can achieve a meaningful learning guarantee when a constant fraction
of episodes are corrupted. Complimentary to the theoretical results, we show
that a neural implementation of FPG achieves strong robust learning performance
on the MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks.

variance} and design algorithms that can tolerate higher variance of rewards.

to use a \emph{filtered} gradient estimator that captures the long-range
correlation of transitions, which is crucial to achieve sublinear learning
guarantees. Finally, our algorithm design leverages the classical concept of
\emph{regularization} to make the proposed algorithms robust. We hope our
theoretical and practical contributions will spur further research on robust

compound states, where a dark exciton is coupled to both even and odd
multi-phonon bundles. In these configurations, we demonstrate that the
decoherence rates are indeed lower than the typical phonon decay rate in
quantum dots. We also show that these compound states are capable of
exhibiting giant Rabi frequencies as well, with values topped at 80 MHz.

in semiconductor nanocavity systems currently under development.

cavity allows for the generation of multi-phonon transitions with an extra
control in the transition frequencies, opening the door for the simultaneous

system identification and design
problems can be formulated as functional optimization problems with
differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has
to resort to numerical methods to compute an approximate solution. This paper
uses a unifying notation to outline some of the techniques used in the
transcription step of simultaneous direct methods (which
discretize-then-optimize) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization
problems. We focus on collocation, integrated residual and Runge-Kutta schemes.
These transcription methods are then applied to a simulation case study to
answer a question that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic, namely: If there are
not enough ventilators, is it possible to ventilate more than one patient on a
single ventilator? The results suggest that it is possible, in principle, to
estimate individual patient parameters sufficiently accurately, using a
relatively small number of flow rate measurements, without needing to
disconnect a patient from the system or needing more than one flow rate sensor.
We also show that it is possible to ensure that two different patients can
indeed receive their desired tidal volume, by modifying the resistance
experienced by the air flow to each patient and controlling the ventilator
pressure.
  A future paper will outline the necessary steps to solve the same case study
using sequential indirect methods (optimize-then-discretize) which predict the
same solution as the direct methods, but with an error that tends to zero as
the discretization and optimization step sizes tend to zero.

to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to investigate if
and to what extent a simplified clinical workflow based on CT alone, allows one
to automatically segment the esophageal tumor with sufficient quality. For this
purpose, we present a fully automatic end-to-end esophageal tumor segmentation
method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed network,
called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages spatial and channel
attention gates in each dense block to selectively concentrate on determinant
feature maps and regions. Dilated convolutional layers are used to manage GPU
memory and increase the network receptive field. We collected a dataset of 792
scans from 288 distinct patients including varying anatomies with \mbox{air
pockets}, feeding tubes and proximal tumors. Repeatability and reproducibility
studies were conducted for three distinct CT scans per distinct patient
($\approx$ 280 patients) and a large clinical study with expert radiologists

hand-corrected, atlas-based methods. Results show that our method achieves a
mean surface to surface distance of $0.53[mm]$ and $0.59[mm]$ for the
repeatability and reproducibility study, respectively. Furthermore, it
significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art, atlas-based methods in terms of
segmentation quality and computational time.

formation evaluation obtained by well-log interpretation while drilling. A
reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to interpret well logs
and capture uncertainties in real-time is necessary for this application. An
iterative ensemble-based method, namely the approximate Levenberg Marquardt
form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML) is integrated in
our formation evaluation workflow. We estimate model parameters, resistivity
and density in addition to boundary locations, and related uncertainties by
reducing the statistical misfit between the measurements from the well logging
tools and the theoretical measurements from the forward tool simulators. The
results of analyzing several synthetic cases with several types of logs
verified that the proposed method can give good estimate of model parameters.
  By comparing the CPU time, we conclude that the proposed method has at least
about 10--125 times lower computational time compare to a common statistical
method, such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo. In addition, the
ensemble-based method can run in parallel on multiple CPUs. Testing the method
on a case inspired from a real field also yielded accurate formation
evaluation. Thus, the proposed method has high potential to be applied to
real-time well-log interpretation (also called density-log interpretation) in
an existing geosteering system.

properties in real-time by using quantitative log analysis tools such as
diagnostic elastic logs. This may help geosteering decisions and improve the

order to address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a

algorithm to disclose the entire NEs once for all. Besides, there is no
research on applying corpus-level information to NER currently. To make up for
the loss of this information, we introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI)
and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics for even better
performance by holistic modeling from sentence-level to corpus-level.

benchmarks which approach or even achieve state-of-the-art. Further empirical
studies show that our proposed corpus-aware features can substantially improve
NER domain adaptation, which demonstrates the surprising advantage of our
proposed corpus-level holistic structure modeling.

languages in the written and oral communication modes. It often results in
language mixing, a.k.a. code-mixing, when a multilingual speaker switches
between multiple languages in a single utterance of a text or speech. This
paper discusses the current state of the NLP research, limitations, and
foreseeable pitfalls in addressing five real-world applications for social good
crisis management, healthcare, political campaigning, fake news, and hate
speech for multilingual societies. We also propose futuristic datasets, models,
and tools that can significantly advance the current research in multilingual
NLP applications for the societal good. As a representative example, we
consider English-Hindi code-mixing but draw similar inferences for other
language pairs.

that can significantly advance the current research in multilingual NLP
applications for the societal good. With MNASG, we propose five promising
datasets for crisis management, healthcare, political campaigning, fake news,
and hate speech for English-Hindi multilingual corpus. We also suggest potential
state-of-the-art NLP models that can be fine-tuned and evaluated on these
datasets. Finally, we argue that the transparency, reliability, and accountabilty
of the MNASG framework can be significantly improved with interpretability and
explainability methods.

references, there is full control over the quality of the data. Also, more

king points in the Cosmic Microwave Background
(CMB), resulting from black hole mergers and black hole evaporation,
respectively, in a previous cycle of the universe, have been predicted as
possible evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model (CCC) introduced by
R. Penrose. We present a high-resolution search for such low-variance circles
in the Planck and WMAP CMB data, and introduce HawkingNet, our machine learning
open-source software based on a ResNet18 algorithm, to search for Hawking
points in the CMB. We find that CMB anomalies, consisting of a single or a few
bright pixels, erroneously lead to regions with many low-variance circles when
applying the search criteria used in previous works [V.G. Gurzadyan, R.
Penrose]. After removing the anomalies from the data no statistically
significant low-variance circles can be found. Concerning Hawking points, also
no statistically significant evidence is found when using a Gaussian
temperature amplitude model over 1 degree opening angle and after accounting
for CMB anomalies. That CMB anomalies themselves might be remnants of Hawking
points is not supported by low-variance and/or high-temperature circles around
them. The absence of such distinct features in the CMB does not disprove CCC
because if the density of such circles and Hawking points is large an averaging
effect would be visible in the CMB, whereas if they are rare they would
nonetheless exist and could be detected in future, higher-resolution CMB
data.
  Finally, we suggest a new approach to the CMB test of CCC taking into account
the expectation that CMB anomalies might be remnants of Hawking points. If such
a correlation holds, then CMB anomalies detected in the present data would be
expected to grow in magnitude in future CMB data, whereas a new class of
structures, not yet detected, should be present in future CMB data.
  We also suggest that future CMB experiments should search for circles of
alternating high and low variance, as these could be remnants of the boundary
of the universe in two consecutive cycles according to CCC.

researchers for its ability to alleviate the data sparsity problem in
recommender systems. However, the existing single-target or dual-target CDR
methods often suffer from two drawbacks, the assumption of at least one rich
domain and the heavy dependence on domain-invariant preference, which are
impractical in real world where sparsity is ubiquitous and might degrade the
user preference learning. To overcome these issues, we propose a
Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model for multi-target
cross-domain recommendation. Unlike traditional CDR methods, MSDCR treats the
multiple relevant domains as all sparse and can simultaneously improve the
recommendation performance in each domain. We propose a Multi-Domain Separation
Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module for
MSDCR to enhance a user's domain-specific aspect preferences in a domain by
transferring the complementary aspect preferences in other domains, during
which the uniqueness of the domain-specific preference can be preserved through
the adversarial training offered by MDSN and the complementarity can be
adaptively determined by GAPE. Meanwhile, we propose a Multi-Domain Adaptation
Network (MDAN) for MSDCR to capture a user's domain-invariant aspect
preference. With the integration of the enhanced domain-specific aspect
preference and the domain-invariant preference, a more comprehensive user
representation can be built to predict the rating in each domain. MSDCR is
designed as a flexible framework and can be extended to both single- and
multi-target CDR scenarios. Experiments on two public datasets validate the
effectiveness of MSDCR, where much better recommendation performance can be
achieved compared with the state-of-the-art single- and dual-target CDR

equivalent conic natural formulations, which can use a much broader class of
exotic cones. We define an exotic cone as a proper cone for which we can
implement tractable logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier oracles
for either the cone or its dual cone. In this paper we introduce Hypatia, a
highly-configurable open-source conic primal-dual interior point solver with a
generic interface for exotic cones. Hypatia is written in Julia and accessible
through JuMP, and currently implements around two dozen useful predefined cones
(some with multiple variants). We define some of Hypatia's exotic cones, and
for conic constraints over these cones, we analyze techniques for constructing
equivalent representations using the standard cones. For optimization problems
from a variety of applications, we introduce natural formulations using these
exotic cones, and we show that the natural formulations are simpler and
lower-dimensional than the equivalent extended formulations. Our computational
experiments demonstrate the potential advantages, especially in terms of solve
time and memory usage, of solving the natural formulations with Hypatia
compared to solving the extended formulations with either Hypatia or MOSEK 9.

definitions for a variety of problems from various applications, and we use

generalize the standard OGS of Sn to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn. We
describe the exchange laws for the generalized standard OGS of Bn, and we
connect it to the Coxeter length and the descent set of Bn.
  We also introduce the notion of the length of an OGS, as a generalization of
the Coxeter length. In the context of the standard OGS of Sn, Shwartz
characterized the elements with length 0. We prove that for the standard OGS
of Bn we have a similar characterization of the elements with length 0.
Finally, we study the order of the elements of the standard OGS of Bn, and we
prove that it is possible to calculate the order of an element of the standard
OGS of Bn, when we know its order in the standard OGS of Sn.

creation and control
of high-performance solid-state telecom photon-spin interfaces. T radiation
damage centres in silicon provide a promising photon-spin interface due to
their narrow O-band optical transition near 1326 nm and long-lived electron and
nuclear spin lifetimes. To date, these defect centres have only been studied as
ensembles in bulk silicon. Here, we demonstrate the reliable creation of high
concentration T centre ensembles in the 220 nm device layer of
silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers by ion implantation and subsequent annealing.
We then develop a method that uses spin-dependent optical transitions to
benchmark the characteristic optical spectral diffusion within these T centre
ensembles. Using this new technique, we show that with minimal optimization to
the fabrication process high densities of implanted T centres localized
$\lesssim$100 nm from an interface display ~1 GHz characteristic levels of
total spectral diffusion.
  We use this result to identify potential solid-state telecom photon-spin
interfaces for the development of global quantum networks.
  Moreover, the macroscopic nature of this result shows that the problem of
spectral diffusion in transition metal flavour centres is not fundamental, but
rather arises from the particular microscopical implementation. This knowledge
will be crucial for the further development of transition metal centre photon
spin interfaces, and will be transferred directly to other transition metal
centres in silicon. Finally, we discuss our results in the context of
quantum network applications and the development of spin-based entanglement
between silicon spin qubits.

a medical image processing technique that
used radio waves to scan the body. It is a tomographic imaging technique,
principally used in the field of radiology. With the advantage of being a
painless diagnostic procedure, MRI allows medical personnel to illustrate clear
pictures of the anatomy and the physiological processes occurring in the body,
thus allowing early detection and treatment of diseases. These images, combined
with image processing techniques may be used in the detection of tumors,
difficult to identify with the naked eye. This digital assignment surveys the
different image processing techniques used in Automated Tumor Detection (ATD).
This assignment initiates the discussion with a comparison of traditional
techniques such as Morphological Tools (MT) and Region Growing Technique (RGT).
This is followed by a comparison of newer technology like Convolutional Neural
Networks (CNN), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Transfer Learning (TL). This
assignment highlights the advantages and disadvantages of these techniques as
well as their applications and future enhancements. Twenty five (25) images
obtained from the Medical Imaging Resource (MIR) database were used to demonstrate
the effectiveness of these techniques. The performance of each technique was
evaluated using the metric of Area Under the Curve (AUC). The comparison
demonstrated that both MT and RGT produced satisfactory results with an AUC of
0.90 and 0.92, respectively. However, these techniques fall short of the ideal
solution as they are sensitive to noise and no prior knowledge of the image
structure is needed to initiate the processing. In contrast, the deeper and
computationally expensive network, CNN, produced remarkable results with an AUC
of 0.98. Furthermore, CNN is capable of processing images with varying
complexity and no prior knowledge of the image structure is needed to initiate
the processing. Lastly, the comparison highlighted the advantage of transfer
learning, which enables the use of pre-trained networks without any additional
training, thus saving time and computational resources.
  From the comparison, it is clear that ATD is still an active area of research
and there is need for further studies to evaluate the performance of these
techniques. Though this assignment discusses twenty five images, it is
suggested that a larger dataset be used to validate the comparison. With the
rising computational power and the increasing need for medical image analysis,
future studies should investigate the performance of these techniques on other
medical image processing tasks.

properties and a randomised algorithm that samples the line combination space.

consistency at mitigating jitter for different activity levels. The analysis is
complemented with planetary injection tests. The parametric selection yields a
RV RMS reduction of less than 10%, while the randomised selection a systematic

efficient collection protocol for Wireless Sensor Networks. The former is the
Bidirectional Link Quality Estimation, which allows nodes to easily and quickly
compute the quality of a link between a pair of nodes. The latter, Hierarchical
Range Sectoring, organizes sensors in different sectors based on their location
within the network. Based on this organization, nodes from each sector are
coordinated to transmit in specific periods of time to reduce the hidden
terminal problem. To evaluate these two mechanisms, a protocol called HBCP

been implemented in TinyOS 2.1, and evaluated in a testbed using TelosB motes.
The results show that the HBCP protocol is able to achieve a very high
reliability, especially in large networks and in scenarios with bottlenecks.
Moreover, it presents a good energy balance among nodes, and is able to
effectively avoid the hidden terminal problem. Finally, the contribution also
shows that the HBCP protocol can be used to obtain very fast data collection in
networks, even those with low bandwidth.

object detectors exploit scene context for recognition differently. In this
paper, we group object detectors into 3 categories in terms of context use: no
context by cropping the input (RCNN), partial context by cropping the
featuremap (two-stage methods) and full context without any cropping
(single-stage methods). We systematically evaluate the effect of context for
each deep detector category. We create a fully controlled dataset for varying
context and investigate the context for deep detectors. We also evaluate
gradually removing the background context and the foreground object on MS COCO.
We demonstrate that single-stage and two-stage object detectors can and will
use the context by virtue of their large receptive field. Thus, choosing the
best object detector may depend on the application context.
  We make the following contributions: (i) We propose a novel metric for
investigating the context that object detectors use; (ii) We create a
fully-controlled dataset for varying context by human annotation; (iii) We
investigate how object detectors respond to the varying context; (iv) We evaluate
object detectors with gradually removed foreground and background context on
COCO.

  Our result for SCP measures include subgaussian inequalities of
bounded-difference type extending classical results by Pemantle and Peres and

Aoun, Banna and Youssef. Under a stronger assumption of the SRP we obtain

  We also treat in detail the special case of independent Bernoulli random
variables conditioned on their sum for which we obtain strengthened estimates,
deriving in particular modified log-Sobolev inequalities, Talagrand's convex
distance inequality and, as corollaries, concentration results for convex
functions and polynomials, as well as improved estimates for matrix-valued
functions. These results generalize inequalities for the uniform measure on
slices of the discrete cube, studied extensively by many authors. Our approach
is based on recent results by Hermon and Salez and a general framework
involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities on the discrete cube, which is of
independent interest.
  We believe that the underlying ideas allowing for extension of classical
inequalities to the matrix-valued setting are of general interest and find
application in other areas of mathematics and computer science. In particular,
our methods provide new guarantees for learning from noisy matrix-valued
inputs, which is of interest in their own right.

variations, as well as a generalization of the Chernoff bound.

prove concentration inequalities which extend classical results by Leger and
Lubotsky, and Bennett, Long, Ostreev and Salek. These estimates are obtained
assuming the strong Rayleigh property or the stochastic covering property,

1951 thesis by T.A. Springer. In this thesis Springer studied the
classification of conjugacy classes in the symplectic group $Sp_n(K)$, where
the commutative field $K$ is of characteristic different from 2. He finds that
each conjugacy class is characterized by a system of invariants. These
invariants are first of all -- as in the case of the general linear group --
irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers, but secondly also
equivalence classes of certain Hermitian forms and of certain quadratic forms.

for Wikipedia that organizes Wikipedia into a collection of graphs layered on

well in terms of quality and user engagement. Balancing simplicity and quality,

million articles in 2.5 hundred languages, more than twice the number of
languages spoken as a native language around the world. As a manifestation of
human knowledge, Wikipedia provides an unprecedented opportunity for entity

structural operations give rise to derivational ambiguities that are missed by

compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed

first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  We achieve this extension of the vectorial interpretation by treating the
control modalities as directional modalities that change the direction of the
flow of meaning in the vector space. As a result, the interpretation of proofs
in the multiplicative subcalculus is extended with an extra dimension, capturing
the effect of the modalities. In the exponential subcalculus, the usual
extension of the space with an extra dimension captures the effect of subexponentials, which we take to delimit the application of the modalities. existing results of Wu et al. (2021). Our algorithms incorporate several novel
techniques to guarantee rationalizability and no (swap-)regret simultaneously,
including a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which
may be of independent interest. We complement our results with a sample
complexity lower bound showing the sharpness of our guarantees.
  The novel algorithmic design leverages three key insights: (1) reducing the
problem to finding rationalizable action profiles and then constructing CCE or
CE from them; (2) using correlated exploration to balance exploration and
exploitation efficiently; and (3) adapting learning rates to adjust the
amount of exploration based on the observed payoffs. We hope our strategies

  WorkingWiki develops further an idea that David Donoho and I explored in a
2008 paper, "Human-Machine Collaboration via Interaction with 'Execution Graphs'". Donogh and I imagined an
environment in which a user would supply some of the work that a program is to
do, and then use the program to process some input to generate output that
relates to what the user has done. WorkingWiki implements this idea with
"templates" that cause it to insert the results of running programs on
textual "snippets" that the user writes in a wiki page. It uses templates to
convert input supplied by the user into output that relates to that input. For
example, a template might cause WorkingWiki to run R code on a snippet of R
code that the user writes to generate a figure for inclusion in a LaTeX
document.

models result in dynamically-bound clusters at neighboring sites. We show that
the dynamics of these clusters in two-dimensional lattices is remarkably
different and richer than that of repulsively-bound on-site clusters in gases
without inter-site interactions. Whereas on-site pairs move in the same lattice
as individual particles, nearest-neighbor dimers perform an interacting quantum
walk in a different lattice geometry, leading to a peculiar dynamics
characterized by more than one time scale. The latter is general for any
lattice geometry, but it is especially relevant in triangular and diamond
lattices, where dimers move resonantly in an effective kagome and Lieb lattice,
respectively. As a result, dimers experience partial quasi-localization due to
an effective flat band, and may move slower than longer clusters. This
surprising link between anomalously slow quantum walk dynamics in these models
and flat-band physics may be readily observed in experiments with lanthanide
atoms.
  We also show that spin dimers in the XXZ model can perform a quantum walk with
two distinct time scales by moving in an effective lattice with both nearest
and next-nearest neighbors interactions. This is a minimal model showing that
flat-band quasi-localization can be triggered by two-site correlations. The
physics of extended-Hubbard and XXZ models with inter-site interactions is
presently unexplored in theory. The results presented here highlight that
already these models can exhibit remarkably strong and robust effects of
flat-band quasi-localization, making them promising candidates for the
observation of related quantum phenomena with cold atoms or quantum simulators
based on mesoscopic devices.

cluster-size thresholds. We find that quasi-localization of two-site clusters
is a general phenomenon that can be observed in any realistic two-dimensional
lattice geometry, while three-site clusters and longer clusters may only be
observed in triangular and diamond lattices.
  In the latter, we find that quasi-localization of longer clusters is
associated with strong bottlenecks in the quantum walk dynamics, which may be
directly observable by measuring the survival probability of clusters with the
inter-site interaction turned on and off.

reliability. To provide low latency data access, replicas are often required to
accept updates without coordination with each other, and the updates are then
propagated asynchronously. This brings the critical challenge of conflict
resolution among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT)
is a principled approach to addressing this challenge. However, existing CRDT
designs are tricky, and hard to be generalized to other data types. A design
framework is in great need to guide the systematic design of new CRDTs.
  To address this challenge, we propose RWF -- the Remove-Win design Framework
for CRDTs. RWF leverages the simple but powerful remove-win strategy to resolve
conflicting updates, and provides generic design for a variety of data
container types. Two exemplar implementations following RWF are given over the
Redis data type store, which demonstrate the effectiveness of RWF. Performance
measurements of our implementations further show the efficiency of CRDT designs
following RWF.
  In addition to CRDT design, RWF paves the way for the evaluation of
replicated data store systems. We propose a performance evaluation framework
for CRDT-based stores, which contains benchmark workloads, evaluation metrics,
and evaluation methods. We perform the evaluation on our Redis implementations
with the framework, and provide detailed performance characterization of
different CRDT designs.
  In summary, RWF is a must-have design framework for CRDTs. It provides a
comprehensive solution to the CRDT design problem, and can be used as the
baseline for the evaluation of replicated data store systems.

https://github.com/zhengdai/phd-thesis.

association studies (GWAS). However, choosing the relevant annotations for
interpreting an association study of a given trait remains challenging. We
describe a statistical model that uses association statistics computed across
the genome to identify classes of genomic element that are enriched or depleted
for loci that influence a trait. The model naturally incorporates multiple
types of annotations. We applied the model to GWAS of 18 human traits,
including red blood cell traits, platelet traits, glucose levels, lipid levels,
height, BMI, and Crohn's disease. For each trait, we evaluated the relevance of
450 different genomic annotations, including protein-coding genes, enhancers,
and DNase-I hypersensitive sites in over a hundred tissues and cell lines. We
show that the fraction of phenotype-associated SNPs that influence protein
sequence ranges from around 2% (for platelet volume) up to around 20% (for LDL
cholesterol); that repressed chromatin is significantly depleted for SNPs
associated with several traits; and that cell type-specific DNase-I
hypersensitive sites are enriched for SNPs associated with several traits (for
example, the spleen in platelet volume). Finally, by re-weighting each GWAS
using information from functional genomics, we increase the number of loci with
high-confidence associations by around 5%.
  We provide a web interface for downloading a pre-computed model for each of the
GWAS studied and for specifying a set of association statistics to be fitted to
a statistical model that identifies genomic classes that are enriched or depleted
for loci that influence a trait. We also provide a R package containing the
statistical model and a web interface for downloading a pre-computed table of
annotations ranked by enrichment/depletion for a set of association statistics.
  The results show that multiple pathways are affected for many complex traits
and provide a functionally annotated list of loci associated with each trait.
Furthermore, by re-weighting each GWAS by a measure of functionality, we increase
the number of loci with high-confidence associations by around 5%. This
approach provides a means of interpreting the results of GWAS and may also be
applied to other -omics disciplines.

used to argue for the presence of a large population of stellar mass black
holes in this region. A core element of the arguments that these objects are
accreting black holes is the claim that neutron stars (NSs) in low mass X-ray
binaries (LMXBs) do not have long transient recurrence times. We demonstrate in
this paper that about half of the known transient LMXBs with clear signatures
for NS primaries have recurrence times in excess of a decade for outbursts at
the sensitivity of MAXI. We furthermore show that, in order to reconcile the
expected total population of NS LMXBs with the observed one and with the
millisecond radio pulsar (MSRP) population of the Galaxy, systems with
recurrence times well in excess of a century for outbursts detectable by
instruments like MAXI must be the dominant population of NS LMXBs, and that few
of these systems have yet been discovered.
  We consider the following transients: the classical burst and transient
neutron star binaries, the dipping and oscillating LMXBs, and the soft X-ray
transients with radio or X-ray pre-outburst observations close to the time of
burst. We treat each class separately in order to discuss the appropriate
upper limits on the population size and to avoid contaminating the sample with
systems which are not representative of the general NS LMXB population.
  For the hard X-ray transients, the tight correlation between pre-outburst
X-ray hardness and outbreak X-ray brightness suggests that the X-ray brightness
of outbursts can be used as a proxy for the mass transfer rate at which the
accretion torque is not sustained. This in turn implies that the recurrence
times observed for these transients are a good representation of the
variability timescales of the transient systems themselves, rather than of
individual neutron star accretion bursts or minor outsbursts, as previously
suggested.
  Based on their characteristics, we estimate that there are at least 10,000
NS LMXBs in the Galaxy, of which about 1000 are expected to be detectable by
MAXI in any outburst phase. We further estimate that about 500 of these
detectable systems are expected to be classical transient systems, and about
300 to be dipping or oscillating systems.

the law of gravity at the low accelerations typical of galactic outskirts. I
consider the feasibility of this wide binary test using the `line velocity'
method. This involves considering only the velocity components along the
direction within the sky plane orthogonal to the systemic proper motion of each
WB.
  I apply this technique to the WB sample of Hernandez et. al. (2019),
carefully accounting for large-angle effects at one order beyond leading. Based
on Monte Carlo trials, the uncertainty in the one-dimensional velocity
dispersion is $\approx 100$ m/s when using sky-projected relative velocities.
Using line velocities reduces this to $\approx 30$ m/s because these are much
less affected by distance uncertainties.
  My analysis does not support the Hernandez et. al. (2019) claim of a clear
departure from Newtonian dynamics beyond a radius of $\approx 10$ kAU, partly
because I use $2\sigma$ outlier rejection to clean their sample first.
Nonetheless, the uncertainties are small enough that existing WB data are
nearly sufficient to distinguish Newtonian dynamics from Modified Newtonian
Dynamics. I estimate that $\approx 1000$ WB systems will be required for this
purpose if using only line velocities.
  In addition to a larger sample, it will also be important to control for
systematics like undetected companions and stellar mass misestimation.
Finally, I note that WB members are, on average, much more massive than those in
the sample of Hernandez et. al. (2019). This could be important because
different studies have found that the mass dependence of $\gamma$ (the power
index of the proposed alternative to Newton's law) is not well constrained or
could be large.
  Future studies should prioritize systematic error control, and include
treatments of multiple or unresolved companions, differential stellar mass
estimation, and careful sky-plane sampling to minimize the impact of large-angle
effects.
  Finally, I emphasize that WB tests are not a way to probe very low
accelerations because the WB ejection mechanism is not yet well understood and
could still be a function of galactic census and depend on other factors like
short-period companions or galactic potential wells.
  In summary, while wide binary tests of gravity are not yet feasible using
existing data sets, I argue that with $\approx 1000$ wide binaries, we may be
able to answer this question

itation of vibrational modes in
molecules and crystals. We show that the circular motion of ions introduces
inertial effects on electrons. In analogy to the classical Coriolis and
centrifugal forces, these effects are the spin-rotation coupling, the
centrifugal field coupling, the centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and the
centrifugal redshift. Depending on the phonon decay, these effects persist for
various picoseconds after excitation. Potential boosting of the effects would
make it a promising platform for vibration-based control of localized quantum
states or chemical reaction barriers.
  From THz phonon modulation, we define time scales for the ion circular motion
and related electron inertia. For CO, CO$_2$, and O$_2$, these time scales are
sub-femtosecond to a few femtoseconds, and are sensitive to molecular
rotation. We show that fast circular motion can activate spin-rotation coupling
in CO and centrifugal field coupling in all three molecules. In N$_2$, similar
time scales indicate partial activation of the centrifugal field coupling. For
the centrifugal spin-orbit coupling and centrifugal redshift, we find N$_2$ and
O$_2$ to be promising candidates given their high transition probabilities.
We further show that the centrifugal field coupling in CO and CO$_2$ is mainly
localizable to the C/O atom and its surrounding chemical bonds. In addition, we
identify that the centrifugal field coupling in CO is sensitive to the end
hydrogen atoms. We explain the robustness of the vibrationally induced
electronic effects to high temperatures and possible experimental detection of
these effects.
  Finally, we propose that the centrifugal redshift could be utilized to
real-time monitor of phonon decay and temperature. We argue that the THz phonon
modulation offers promising time scales for vibrationally induced modification
of chemical reactions, chemical bond breaking, and rotation-induced charge
separation. Last, we explain that the spin-rotation coupling could be switched
on and off by controlling the phonon decay.

ting theory was introduced by Adachi, Iyama and
Reiten at the beginning of the last decade and quickly became one of the most
active areas of research in the representation theory of finite dimensional
algebras. The aim of these notes is two-fold. On the one hand, we want to give
a friendly introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory to anyone with a small
background in representation theory. On the other, we want to fill the apparent
gap for a survey on the subject by collecting in one place many of the most
important results in $\tau$-tilting theory.
  Let $A$ be a finite dimensional algebra over a field. We start by introducing
the basic concepts of $\tau$-tilting theory, such as $\tau$-tilting modules,
$\tau$-tilting variables or (upper) $\tau$-tilting cones. Throughout the
notes, we illustrate all concepts with the help of examples, often using
quivers and their representation theory. In Section 2 we introduce the
notion of a $\tau$-tilting cone for a triangulated category ${\mathcal D}$. We
illustrate this with the help of the derivation category of hereditary algebra,
introducing the terms maximally tilting module and torsion theory.
  Section 3 is devoted to the connection between $\tau$-tilting theory and
stably equivalent algebras. In Section 4 we introduce the notion of
quasitilted algebra and study its connection with $\tau$-tilting theory. We
end the notes with Section 5, devoted to the extension of $\tau$-tilting
theory to higher preprojective tilting modules and quasitilted algebras.
  It is our hope that these notes will be useful to both the seasoned
researcher and the newcomer to the subject. For the latter, they contain what
is needed to start working in $\tau$-tilting theory, while for the former they
offer a number of new examples and insights to consider.
  Finally, let us point out that during the writing of these notes a number of
new examples and results have been obtained. Some of these are contained in
the text while others are left to the reader as exercises (see Exercises 2 and
3). We hope that the notes will encourage the reader to work through them and
obtain new results in return.

contributions to improving diversity in dialogue generation. First, we propose
a novel metric which uses Natural Language Inference (NLI) to measure the
semantic diversity of a set of model responses for a conversation. We evaluate
this metric using an established framework (Tevet and Berant, 2021) and find

neutral relation for measuring this diversity and that incorporating the NLI
model's confidence achieves state-of-the-art results. Second, we demonstrate
how to iteratively improve the semantic diversity of a sampled set of responses
via a new generation procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which
results in an average 137% increase in NLI Diversity compared to standard

use expensive sensor setups and complex processing pipeline, limiting their
availability and robustness. To address these issues, we introduce a novel deep
learning based action recognition framework for classifying dangerous lane
change behavior in short video clips captured by a monocular camera. We
designed a deep spatiotemporal classification network that uses pre-trained

feature extractor for this task. The Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) and

semi-naturalistic lane change dataset with annotated risk labels. A
comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art feature extractors was carried out

construct the models of rotating very low-mass stellar objects that may or may

source. The rotation is not limited to being slow so the effect of the

luminosity, are obtained for different values of angular momentum. It is shown
that if the angular momentum exceeds the threshold $J_0=8.85\times 10^{48}{\rm
erg}~{\rm s}$ the critical curve is broken up into two branches with lower and
higher degeneracy because of the mass-shedding limit. Based on the results, we
model mechano-thermal evolutions of substellar objects, in which cooling, as
well as mass/angular momentum reductions, are followed for two simplified
cases. The case with such external braking mechanisms as magnetized wind or
magnetic braking is mainly controlled by the spin-down timescale. The other
case with interior braking by the visit of a tidal companion is mainly
controlled by the orbital decay timescale. We show how the critical curve with
lower (higher) mass but higher (lower) degeneracy contributes to the modeling
of a binary neutron star (NS) or a white dwarf (WD) plus WD system,
respectively. The merging of the two objects in the case of a WD plus WD
system is not considered. For all of the considered cases, the effect of
rotation on the occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning is not negligible,
and thus it should be considered in future more general modeling.

They have a wide range of applications and are often visualized as a 2-layered
drawing, where each set of objects is visualized as a set of vertices (points)
on one of the two parallel horizontal lines and the relationships are
represented by edges (simple curves) between the two lines connecting the
corresponding vertices. One of the common objectives in such drawings is to
minimize the number of crossings this, however, is computationally expensive
and may still result in drawings with so many crossings that they affect the
readability of the drawing. We consider a recent approach to remove crossings
in such visualizations by splitting vertices, where the goal is to find the
minimum number of vertices to be split to obtain a planar drawing. We show that
determining whether a planar drawing exists after splitting at most $k$
vertices is fixed parameter tractable in $k$.
  Another objective in visualizations is to minimize the length of the edges
representing the relationships. For square drawings, where the distance between
two vertices representing a relationship $e$ is equal to the label size of $e$,
we show that determining whether such a drawing with at most $k$ edge extensions
is possible is fixed parameter tractable in $k$.
  Finally, we consider both objectives simultaneously and determine the
complexity of the corresponding optimization problem and the decision problem
for bounded and unbounded number of vertex splits.
  Throughout our work we construct parameterized algorithms and exact enumerators
based on Extended Grid extensions of Dynamic Planar Point-Finding and Planar
Monotone Dualization.
  We show that all our algorithms and enumerators can be implemented in
polynomial time and thus are fixed-parameter efficient.
  We also investigate the relationship between vertex splits and geometric
degeneracies and show that many problems related to bipartite drawings can be
reduced to the problem we consider.

standard Cartesian Decomposition of the wreath product $G=G_{1}\wr S_{n}$ is
the set $\left\{ X_{1},X_{2},\cdots,X_{n}\right\} $ where $X_{i}=X\text{ }$if
$i=\sigma\left( j\right) $ and $X_{i}=Y$ if $i\neq \sigma \left( j\right) $ for
all $j=$ $1,2,\cdots,n$.
  Let $H$ be a diagonal subgroup of $G$. Let $\theta :X\rightarrow Y$ be an
isomorphism of groups. Define $\phi :X_{i_{1}}\rightarrow X_{i_{2}}$ by $\phi
=\theta $ if $X_{i_{1}}=X_{i_{2}}$ and $\phi$ is an isomorphism from $X_{i_{1}}$
to $X_{i_{2}}$ such that $\phi \left( x\right) =\theta \left( x\right) $ for all
$x\in X$ if $X_{i_{1}}\neq X_{i_{2}}$. Then $\phi $ is an embedding of the
subgroups $X_{i_{1}}$ and $X_{i_{2}}$. Let $K=\left\langle \phi \right\rangle $ be
the subgroup of $G$ generated by $\phi $.

wreath product $G=G_{1}\wr S_{n}$ in the product action using the Cartesian
Decomposition and we gave the rules for this embedding. Also we showed how $H$

systems are seen as a promising technology for providing very high data rates
in increased user-density scenarios. Spatial non-stationarities and visibility
regions (VRs) appear across the XL-MIMO array since its large dimension is of
the same order as the distances to the user-equipments (UEs). Due to the
increased density of UEs in typical applications of XL-MIMO systems and the
scarcity of pilots, the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling
algorithms become challenging. In this paper, we propose a joint RA and
scheduling protocol, namely non-overlapping VR XL- MIMO (NOVR-XL) RA protocol,
which takes advantage of the different VRs of the UEs for improving RA
performance, besides seeking UEs with non-overlapping VRs to be scheduled in
the same payload data pilot resource. Our results reveal that the proposed
scheme achieves significant gains in terms of sum rate compared with
traditional RA schemes, as well as reducing access latency and improving
connectivity performance as a whole.
  The proposed NOVR-XL RA protocol is designed for XL-MIMO systems with large
number of base station antennas compared to the number of UEs. Due to the
large number of XL-MIMO antennas, the UEs' VRs are not uniformally distributed
across the entire spectrum, but are centered around their location. This
non-stationary spacial distribution of VRs can be used in order to improve the
performance of the RA protocol. In this work we propose a novel RA protocol
which assigns UEs with non-overlapping VRs the same piloting resources, resulting
in a significant reduction of the access latency as compared to traditional RA
protocols. The simulation results reveal an increase in the sum rate of up to
30% and an order of magnitude reduction in access latency.

  In this paper, we have investigated the spectral or frequency shift in a
gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer. A rapid shift in the spectrum or frequency
around the anomaly point is usually observed in the gyroscope. Due to some
confusing explanations about the anomaly point, detailed investigation on this
shift is necessary. It is well known that the counter propagating beams in a
Sagnac interferometer suffer equal and opposite Doppler shifts. The sum of these
Doppler shifts becomes zero. But in the case of the gyroscopic Sagnac
interferometer, the beams suffer additional gyroscopic frequency shift in
addition to their usual counter clock wise shift due to rotation of the gyroscope
around its vertical axis. This additional frequency shift causes the anomaly in
the interferometer. On analysis of the problem it is observed that the anomaly
point in the gyroscope is not a pure anomaly point but it is an anomaly point
attached with a spectral or frequency shift.

in free space as compared to water. So, measurement of the spectral shift in the

  Which human rules should we use to improve a machine learning model? On one
hand, using more rules gives a higher chance to clean out noisy data. On the
other hand, it increases the cost of labeling. Moreover, not all human rules
are effective (with respect to accuracy and trust score) and relevant (with
respect to unexpected behavior). To address these issues, we propose a language
model-based filtering mechanism which removes less effective and less relevant
rules. Then we evaluate different combinations of human rules on corrupted
versions of the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets. We get an improvement in
accuracy and trust score with fewer labels than without filtering.

of differential privacy (DP) in the
context of graph-structured data. We discuss the formulations of DP applicable
to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by an absence of a
single, well-established formulation of DP in graph settings. This issue
extends to the domain of GNNs, rendering private machine learning on
graph-structured data a challenging task. A lack of prior systematisation work
motivated us to study graph-based learning from a privacy perspective. In this
work, we systematise different formulations of DP on graphs, discuss challenges
and promising applications, including the GNN domain. We compare and separate
works into graph analysis tasks and graph learning tasks with GNNs. Finally, we
conclude our work with a discussion of open questions and potential directions
for further research in this area.
  We make the following three key contributions: (i) We propose a novel
classification of graph analysis tasks and graph learning tasks with GNNs based
on the underlying data distribution -- traditional and modern (complex) settings.
(ii) We study (individual) DP and its relaxations (group and central DP) in the
context of graph-structured data. We discuss challenges arising from
individual data connections and the need for a well-defined graph algorithm
complexity. (iii) We study the privacy of GNNs,  review recent work on
differentially private GNN training and output privacy of GNNs. The following
works build the foundation for our research: Tosh et al. [1] provide an
overview of DP on graphs while Huang et al. [2] survey the privacy of GNNs. Our
work complements these two works by providing a systematic classification of
graph analysis tasks and algorithms studies based on the underlying data
distribution as well as individual and central DP in the context of graph-structured
data.

set of control points, we construct a parametric curve that represents a road
network, which defines the dynamic driving task an automated lane keep system
equipped vehicle has to perform. Changing control points has global influence
on the resulting road geometry. Our approach uses search to find a set of
control points that results in a challenging road geometry, eventually forcing
the vehicle to leave the intended path. We evaluated our approach in three
different search-configurations regarding test efficiency and practical
applicability for automatic virtual testing of an automated lane keep system.
While the results are promising, search still lacks the efficiency to be
practically applicable. Therefore, we suggest to use it as a component in a
two-stage process: The derivative of the resulting road geometry can be used to
pre-select candidate control points that only cause local deviation of the
vehicle from the intended path. In a second step, the driver behavior model
based on physical modeling of a vehicle can be used to filter these candidates
and directly propose test failures including the exact driving scenario.
Therefore, we provide a set of test scenarios which can be used to improve the
generation process outlined in this paper.

simulating the otherwise difficult-to-compute dynamics of quantum many-body
systems. In this work we derive, within the positive-P phase-space formalism, a
new stochastic hydrodynamic method for the description of interacting Bose
gases. It goes beyond existing hydrodynamic approaches, such as superfluid
hydrodynamics or generalized hydrodynamics, in its capacity to simulate the
full quantum dynamics of these systems: it possesses the ability to compute
non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena.
Using this description, we derive a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme
which is able to simulate such non-equilibrium situations for longer times than
the full positive-P approach, at the expense of approximating the treatment of
quantum fluctuations, and show that this linearized scheme can be directly
connected with existing Bogoliubov approaches. Furthermore, we go on to
demonstrate the usefulness and advantages of this formalism by exploring the
correlations that arise in a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its
predictions to other established quantum many-body approaches.
  We find that the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme can simulate
finite-size effects in quantum shocks, while the full positive-P approach is
capable of describing the dynamics of quantum gases within superfluid systems
such as rotating systems and quasichannels.
  Finally, we explain why stochastic hydrodynamics can be particularly
advantageous when considering the dynamics of dilute Bose gases, for which
many-body wave-function Monte Carlo methods are not as effective as they are
for larger and more interacting particle numbers.
  This new stochastic-hydrodynamics approach could, thus, open up new
perspectives on the the investigation of quantum many-body physics and could
assist in the evaluation of the accuracy of other theoretical approaches with
relatively less computational resources.

this paper proposes the end-to-end proposal generation method named DCAN to
aggregate context on two levels, namely, boundary level and proposal level, for

higher or lower plasma densities are called blobs and holes. Measurements show

generated. If the ELM-filament itself is captured on a q=3 surface, the
filtration effect of the q=3 surface needs to be sufficiently weak to create a
PTM. If this ELM-filament is partially reflected from the q=3 surface, a
typically shorter-lived PTM equivalent signature can be measured. If the
filtration effect of the q=3 surface is too strong, the ELM-filament will be
mirrored on the q=3 surface and no long-lived PTM will be observed.

considerable progress in this area in the past years, measuring and comparing
the effectiveness of fuzzers is still an open research question. In software
testing, the gold standard for evaluating test quality is mutation analysis,
assessing the ability of a test to detect synthetic bugs; if a set of tests
fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect real bugs. Mutation
analysis subsumes various coverage measures and provides a large and diverse
set of faults that can be arbitrarily hard to trigger and detect, thus
preventing the problems of saturation and overfitting. Unfortunately, the cost
of traditional mutation analysis is exorbitant for fuzzing, as mutations need
independent evaluation.
  In this paper, we apply modern mutation analysis techniques that pool
multiple mutations; allowing us, for the first time, to evaluate and compare
fuzzers with mutation analysis. We introduce an evaluation bench for fuzzers
and apply it to a number of popular fuzzers and subjects. In a comprehensive
evaluation, we show how it allows us to assess fuzzer performance and measure
the impact of improved techniques. While we find that today's fuzzers can
detect only a small percentage of mutations, this should be seen as a challenge
for future research -- notably in improving (1) detecting failures beyond
generic crashes (2) triggering mutations (and thus faults).
  Overall, mutation analysis is ready to answer more of the questions of the
fuzzing community; and a well-designed evaluation bench is crucial for
drawing conclusions from evaluation data.
  We advocate for MMAF -- a multipooled multiple-input multiple-output
mutation-analysis framework -- to evaluate and compare fuzzers and subjects.
We provide a Python-based implementation of MMAF, including a bench with multiple
mutators for covering a large diversity of faults and a set of popular fuzzers
